source_text: Medicum dicit Dominum Iesum. Non sanos vocat sed peccatores. Herbae legis in schola medici componuntur.
orientation: Origen is opening a new homily, speaking in his own voice about Christ as a physician who calls sinners, not the healthy.
pass_a_gloss: Medicum [he] calls [the] Lord Jesus. Not [the] healthy [he] calls but sinners. [The] herbs of [the] law in [the] school of [the] physician are put together.

choices.why: The noun is predicate accusative; English needs the article to mark the role rather than a specific known physician.

choices.english: He does not call the healthy but sinners
choices.why: Keeps the exact negation and contrast, with 'the healthy' as a class and 'sinners' as the object of the call.
rejected: He calls not the righteous but sinners
It is not the healthy he calls but sinners

choices.why: Preserves the botanical metaphor of the law's contents as medicinal plants, matching the physician image.

choices.english: are compounded in the school of the physician
choices.why: Keeps the passive verb and the image of a medical school where remedies are prepared; 'compounded' fits the pharmaceutical sense.
rejected: are mixed in the physician's school
are prepared in the school of the physician

bible_refs.note: Non sanos vocat sed peccatores echoes Jesus' saying that he came not to call the righteous but sinners, and that the healthy do not need a physician.

pass_b_english: He calls the Lord Jesus a physician. He does not call the healthy but sinners. The herbs of the law are compounded in the school of the physician.
